title: Kilroy v. Commissioner
subject: Inventor's Trade or Business Under Section 174
summary: Kilroy v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1980-489, is a U.S. Tax Court decision holding that an independent inventor who patents and markets inventions over several years is engaged in a trade or business under I.R.C. § 174 before earning income. The Court allowed the research-related share of office expenses under Section 174, costs that remain excluded from Section 41 computations.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background
Procedural Posture and Factual Context

In the jurisprudence governing United States federal research and development (R&D) tax incentives, Kilroy v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1980-489, 41 T.C.M. (CCH) 292 (1980)—preceded by earlier litigation involving the same taxpayer in Kilroy v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1973-7, 32 T.C.M. (CCH) 27 (1973)—stands as a foundational United States Tax Court decision delineating the boundaries of an independent inventor's "trade or business" and the scope of deductible research and experimental (R&E) expenditures under Internal Revenue Code (I.R.C.) Section 174. The petitioners, Oliver B. Kilroy and Alice W. Kilroy, were husband and wife residing in Tucson, Arizona; Alice W. Kilroy was a party solely because she filed joint returns with her husband. Oliver B. Kilroy was an individual inventor who, during the years at issue, also managed his personal investments and engaged in mining exploration via exploratory core drilling, and whose patent applications and disclosure documents covered an interlocked pallet and container system, a hydraulic mining system for underground (particularly coal) mining, a substance exhibiting anti-fungal properties, a method for preparing an anti-viral agent, and a substance effective against certain allergies.

For taxable years 1972 and 1973 (with 1969 also at issue because of a net operating loss carryback from 1972), the taxpayer claimed deductions—directly and through Kilroy Enterprises, a limited partnership that he, his wife, and his children formed late in 1972 to acquire, develop, and market mining ventures and patent claims—for research and experimental expenditures under I.R.C. § 174, for miscellaneous office expenses relating to his inventing activities under Section 174, for office expenses relating to his mining activities under I.R.C. § 617, and, in the alternative, for those miscellaneous expenses under I.R.C. §§ 162 or 212. Although the taxpayer had received no income from his inventing activities and had substantial outside income, he did not operate without staff or facilities: at various times he and Kilroy Enterprises employed a microbiologist, patent attorneys, and a consulting economist in connection with his inventions, contacted consulting engineers about their marketability, and incurred office expenses, and he sought to monetize his inventions by selling licenses and marketing them to packing, pharmaceutical, oil, gas, and mining companies. Along with direct research and experimental costs, the taxpayer claimed deductions for miscellaneous office expenses (incidental expenses) incurred by him and by Kilroy Enterprises in connection with the inventing and mining activities; the opinion does not identify telephone or travel charges as items claimed by the taxpayer, and mentions telephone, travel, and labor costs only in describing what the Court had allowed in a prior case.
The Internal Revenue Service Challenge

The Commissioner of Internal Revenue disallowed the taxpayer's claimed deductions—in a statutory notice of deficiency dated April 1, 1976, determining deficiencies of $5,839 for 1969, $3,585 for 1972, and $725 for 1973—on trade-or-business and expense-allocation grounds. First, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) challenged the threshold eligibility of the taxpayer's activities, asserting that the expenditures were not paid or incurred "in connection with his trade or business" as mandated by I.R.C. § 174(a)(1). The Commissioner determined that the taxpayer was not in the business of inventing or mining in 1972, that Kilroy Enterprises was not in the business of inventing or mining in 1973, and that no office expenses incurred in connection with any of the taxpayer's activities in 1972 and 1973 were deductible; respondent emphasized that the taxpayer's gross receipts from inventing had been negligible, and the record included the Tax Court's 1973 decision against the same taxpayer for 1965, 1966, 1967, and 1970, years in which he had no patents or patent applications and made only isolated attempts at inventing.

Second, the Commissioner contested the deductibility of the indirect office expenses and their allocation among the taxpayer's activities. The IRS did not dispute the research and experimental character or the amount of the core expenditures—respondent admitted that the taxpayer incurred research and experimental expenses of $22,986 in 1972 and that Kilroy Enterprises incurred research and experimental expenses of $20,605 in 1973—but argued that the miscellaneous office expenses were not deductible under Section 174; that the office expenses relating to mining were not deductible under I.R.C. § 617 because they were not directly related to exploratory drilling (although respondent allowed Section 617 deductions for some of the drilling expenses themselves, it treated the office expenses as "too indirect"); that none of these expenses qualified under I.R.C. §§ 162 or 212; that the expenses attributed to managing personal assets were not shown to qualify under Section 212; and that, because the taxpayer had not established which portion of the incidental expenses belonged to each activity, none of them should be deductible.
Governing Statutory and Regulatory Framework

The dispute in Kilroy centered on I.R.C. § 174, enacted by Congress in 1954 to eliminate uncertainty in the tax accounting treatment of research and experimental outlays and to place nascent, pre-revenue innovators on an equal tax footing with established industrial enterprises holding ongoing research departments. During the tax years at issue, and prior to the mandatory capitalization and amortization amendments enacted by the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, I.R.C. § 174(a)(1) permitted a taxpayer to elect to treat R&E expenditures paid or incurred during the taxable year "in connection with his trade or business" as current deductions not chargeable to a capital account. The statutory architecture governing Kilroy and its subsequent application to the I.R.C. § 41 Credit for Increasing Research Activities—first enacted in 1981 (as § 44F under the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981, later redesignated as § 41), the year after the Kilroy ruling—operates across three interlocking legal tiers.

The first statutory tier concerns the critical distinction between the "in connection with" standard of I.R.C. § 174(a)(1) and the stricter "carrying on" standard of I.R.C. § 162(a) and I.R.C. § 41(b)(1). Under Sections 162(a) and 41(b)(1), expenditures are eligible only if paid or incurred in carrying on an existing, presently operating trade or business. By contrast, under the landmark Supreme Court precedent of Snow v. Commissioner, 416 U.S. 500 (1974), Congress deliberately utilized the broader phrase "in connection with his trade or business" in Section 174(a)(1) to dilute the strict requirement of an already-functioning commercial operation, thereby allowing pre-operating and start-up ventures to deduct R&E costs prior to generating revenue. However, as clarified in Kilroy, the Tax Court, citing Snow, stated that the concept of "trade or business" in Section 174 is similar to that in Section 162, and treated whether an individual is engaged in a trade or business for profit as a matter of intent to be determined from the facts (citing Treas. Reg. § 1.183-2(a) and Hirsch v. Commissioner), noting that conducting an activity at a loss does not by itself preclude it from being a business (citing Doggett v. Burnet); the further requirement of a "realistic prospect"—comprising both objective intent and operational capability—of commercially exploiting the research results was articulated in later case law rather than in Kilroy.

The second statutory tier governs the substantive scope of direct and indirect R&E expenditures. Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1) defines R&E expenditures as costs incurred in the "experimental or laboratory sense," encompassing all costs incident to the development or improvement of a product, pilot model, process, formula, invention, technique, patent, or similar property intended for internal business use or for sale, lease, or license. Crucially, unlike I.R.C. § 41(b)—which restricts credit-eligible Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) strictly to direct in-house wages, direct supplies, computer leasing, and 65 percent of eligible contract research—Section 174 encompasses both direct costs and indirect overhead costs incidental to the research effort. Regulatory and judicial authorities confirm that eligible indirect Section 174 expenditures include administrative costs under Rev. Rul. 73-20, product development department overhead under Rev. Rul. 73-275, heat, light, and power under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-4(c), and, as explicitly adjudicated in Kilroy, the portion of office expenses relating to the taxpayer's inventing activities (the Court noting that it had previously allowed Section 174 deductions for utility expenses such as the telephone, travel expenses, and labor costs incurred in invention activities, citing Magee v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1973-271).

The third statutory tier addresses the interplay between modern Section 41 credit claims and post-2021 Section 174 capitalization rules (as modified for domestic research by I.R.C. § 174A beginning in 2025). Because I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(A) explicitly requires that qualified research consist of activities with respect to which expenditures may be treated as expenses under Section 174, satisfying the Kilroy Section 174 thresholds is the mandatory first prong of the Section 41 Four-Part Test. Furthermore, under current United States tax law—where, following the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (Pub. L. 119-21, enacted July 4, 2025), domestic R&E expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024 may again be deducted currently under new I.R.C. § 174A (or, at the taxpayer's election, capitalized and amortized over not less than 60 months), foreign R&E expenditures remain subject to mandatory fifteen-year amortization under Section 174, and expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021 and before January 1, 2025 were subject to mandatory five-year domestic amortization—Kilroy's inclusion of research-related indirect office expenses within Section 174 creates a double-edged compliance reality. Specifically, ancillary expenses that Kilroy swept into Section 174 must now be identified, allocated to research, and (for foreign research and for 2022–2024 expenditures) capitalized, even though those exact same indirect expenses remain statutorily excluded from generating a tax credit under Section 41.
The Tax Court's Final Holding

The United States Tax Court ruled in favor of the taxpayer on the core legal principle that an independent inventor's ongoing activities to develop and exploit inventions through royalties or patent sales constitute a valid trade or business under I.R.C. § 174. Writing that "[t]he concept of 'trade or business' in section 174 is similar to that in section 162," the Court held that whether a taxpayer is engaged in a trade or business is a question of intent determined from the totality of the facts and circumstances. Citing Louw v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1971-326, in a footnote and relying principally on Avery v. Commissioner, 47 B.T.A. 538 (1942), the Court reaffirmed that the "exploitation of inventions through royalties, sales of patents, or otherwise may constitute a business," and found that the taxpayer's actions over a period of years—applying for and receiving numerous U.S. and foreign patents beginning in 1972, distributing literature about his inventions to various companies, and seeking advice from consulting engineers on their market potential—established that he was engaged in the business of inventing for profit, even though neither he nor the partnership had yet received income from it and he had substantial outside income; the Court distinguished its 1973 decision against the same taxpayer, which involved only an isolated instance of research, and held his research and experimental expenses deductible under Section 174 whether incurred directly or through the partnership. Additionally, the Court held that the percentage of the office expenses of the taxpayer and the partnership relating to their inventing activities is deductible under Section 174—observing that it had previously allowed Section 174 deductions for "utility expenses, such as the telephone, travel expenses, and labor costs incurred in invention activities" and that Congress could easily have excluded office expenses had it so intended—and that office expenses relating to exploratory core drilling were deductible under Section 617 as reasonably connected with preparations for extracting ore (citing Estate of DeBie v. Commissioner, 56 T.C. 876 (1971)). Relying on the parties' stipulation and Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930), the Court allowed 90 percent of the incidental expenses as relating to the inventing and mining activities and disallowed the remaining 10 percent attributed to the management of personal assets, because the taxpayer, who did not appear to testify, offered no evidence of what that activity encompassed; decision was entered under Rule 155.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

While Kilroy v. Commissioner established favorable precedent regarding the viability of a licensing-based inventing business and the eligibility of research-related office expenses under Section 174 (with the taxpayer losing only on the 10 percent of incidental expenses attributed to managing personal assets, for lack of evidence), the litigation—viewed together with the taxpayer's earlier loss in T.C. Memo. 1973-7 and the broader body of Tax Court jurisprudence applying Kilroy across Section 174 and Section 41 disputes—exposes critical legal, technical, contractual, and evidentiary deficiencies that routinely trigger IRS audit disallowances. An exhaustive examination of the case record and its doctrinal progeny reveals four core failure mechanisms.
Failure to Establish Trade or Business Continuity vs. Passive Investment or Sporadic Activity

The primary catalyst for the IRS challenge in Kilroy was the absence of any income from the taxpayer's inventing activities, viewed against his history: in the earlier case, T.C. Memo. 1973-7, covering 1965, 1966, 1967, and 1970, the taxpayer had no patents or patent applications and made only isolated attempts at inventing. Because the taxpayer's gross receipts from inventing were negligible, he had substantial outside income, and patent monetization yields lumpy, infrequent revenue rather than steady daily receipts, the Commissioner treated the activity as falling short of a trade or business; the Court rejected that view, explaining that this type of business may take time to produce income, that the taxpayer's outside income was irrelevant, and that, unlike the isolated instance of research in the earlier case, the record now showed sustained patenting and substantial marketing efforts.

In Kilroy and subsequent jurisprudence—most notably Green v. Commissioner, 83 T.C. 667 (1984), Kantor v. Commissioner, 998 F.2d 1514 (9th Cir. 1993), and Spellman v. Commissioner—the determinative evidentiary failure occurs when a taxpayer cannot prove its intent to engage in a trade or business for profit (which the taxpayer in Kilroy succeeded in proving through patents and substantial marketing efforts over a period of years) or, under the later decisions, both the objective intent and the practical capability to enter into an active trade or business with the fruits of the research—a capability test that Kilroy itself did not articulate. While Kilroy confirmed that licensing and royalty exploitation can constitute a business if the taxpayer personally and continuously conducts the research and licensing activities over a period of years, taxpayers fail this threshold through two recurring structural missteps. First, taxpayers incur disallowance when they conduct isolated, sporadic inventing or engineering activities without a structured commercial exploitation plan, business ledger, or continuous multi-year operational history. Second, taxpayers fail when they structure their operations as passive R&D partnerships or joint ventures that immediately assign or grant pre-existing exclusive options over all resulting intellectual property to an outside operating corporation.

As the IRS Office of Chief Counsel emphasized in analyzing Kilroy alongside Green in IRS Field Attorney Advice 20055203F, when an entity merely contributes capital or holds bare legal title while another enterprise retains absolute control over marketing and manufacturing, the taxpayer lacks a "realistic prospect" of entering a trade or business and is disqualified as a mere passive investor. Furthermore, for purposes of the I.R.C. § 41 tax credit, relying solely on Kilroy's Section 174 "in connection with" standard is fatal because Section 41(b)(1) demands that the taxpayer be actively "carrying on" a trade or business at the exact time the expenses are incurred, unless the taxpayer strictly satisfies the narrow start-up rules for in-house research expenses under I.R.C. § 41(b)(4).
Conflation of Routine Mining Exploration and Developmental Engineering with Experimental Research

A technical boundary illustrated by the Kilroy litigation—although the Court did not disallow any expenses on this ground—is the line between mineral exploration and experimental research. The taxpayer's activities involved exploratory core drilling for minerals alongside his inventing activities; consistent with that statutory separation, he claimed the mining-related office expenses under I.R.C. § 617 rather than Section 174, respondent allowed Section 617 deductions for some of the drilling expenses, and the Court allowed the related office expenses under Section 617 as reasonably connected with preparations for extracting ore. Under I.R.C. § 174(d) (subsequently recodified at § 174(c)(2)) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(c), expenditures for the exploration of mineral, oil, or gas deposits—specifically outlays to ascertain the existence, location, extent, or quality of any deposit—are expressly excluded from Section 174 and are governed instead by specialized extractive provisions such as I.R.C. § 617.

Beyond the statutory mineral exploration bar, taxpayers routinely fail to segregate developmental engineering where operational feasibility is already established from true experimentation. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1), costs qualify only if incurred to eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product. When a taxpayer incurs costs in routine engineering, equipment modification where capability and method are known, or standard commercial production setup, the Tax Court disallows the deduction for lack of technological uncertainty. When escalated to an I.R.C. § 41 credit claim, this technical failure becomes even more pronounced: the taxpayer must not only prove technological uncertainty under Section 174, but must also prove under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) that "substantially all" (at least 80 percent) of the research activities constituted elements of a structured process of experimentation—evaluating alternatives through modeling, simulation, or systematic trial and error—relying on the principles of physical, biological, engineering, or computer sciences to improve the functionality, performance, reliability, or quality of a defined business component.
Insufficient Contemporaneous Substantiation and Failure of Proximate Nexus for Indirect Costs

Although Kilroy noted that the Tax Court had previously allowed Section 174 deductions for "utility expenses, such as the telephone, travel expenses, and labor costs incurred in invention activities" (citing Magee v. Commissioner) and held the inventing-related portion of the taxpayer's office expenses deductible under Section 174, the case underscores the acute evidentiary vulnerability of mixed-use and indirect costs. For an independent inventor or engineering group operating without a segregated laboratory facility, utility bills, telephone charges, and travel outlays inherently commingle personal, general administrative, commercial marketing, and experimental activities.

In Kilroy, the Tax Court allowed only the percentage of office expenses that related to the inventing activities; it rejected respondent's argument that the lack of an activity-by-activity allocation barred any deduction, instead treating the parties' stipulation about the taxpayer's time (10 percent managing personal assets, with the remainder spent on inventing and mining) as a reasonable basis under Cohan v. Commissioner to allocate 90 percent of the incidental expenses to the inventing and mining activities, while disallowing the 10 percent attributed to managing personal assets because no testimony or evidence explained what that activity encompassed. When taxpayers present unallocated utility invoices, generalized travel receipts, or retrospective oral testimony without contemporaneous logs tying each telephone call, trip, or utility charge to a specific experimental hypothesis or developmental project, the IRS disallows the expenses for lack of substantiation under I.R.C. § 6001. Moreover, a severe legal failure occurs when taxpayers attempt to carry Kilroy-eligible indirect expenses—such as telephone, utilities, travel, and administrative overhead—into their I.R.C. § 41 QRE computation. Under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b), indirect overhead, travel, telephone, and general utility costs are strictly barred from QRE treatment, regardless of how closely tied they are to the research.
Contractual Deficiencies: Funded Research, Substantial Rights, and Economic Risk

In evaluating whether an inventor, engineering firm, or joint venture participant qualifies for R&D tax benefits under the Kilroy framework and I.R.C. § 41, contractual allocation of financial risk and intellectual property rights frequently proves fatal. Under Section 174, specifically Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(2) and (b)(3), research costs incurred in connection with the construction or manufacture of depreciable property by another are deductible only if made "upon the taxpayer's order and at his risk." Similarly, in joint venture structures analyzed in later authorities citing Kilroy, a participant can claim Section 174 deductions only if it acts as an equal participant sharing the economic risk of the venture rather than reimbursing or being reimbursed on a risk-free basis.

Under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), this contractual scrutiny intensifies into the Funded Research Exclusion and the Mirror Rules governing in-house versus contract research. With respect to economic risk and contingency of payment under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2) and § 1.41-4A(d)(1), if a researcher performs R&D for a client under a fixed-price or milestone contract where payment is not contingent on technical success, the research is treated as funded, disqualifying the researcher from claiming QREs. Conversely, if payment is contingent on technical success—verified through specific contractual barometers for success, quality assurance procedures, and mechanisms for inspection, evaluation, and acceptance—the payor is treated as purchasing "the product or result" of the research rather than funding the research itself; thus, the payor is barred from claiming contract research QREs, and only the researcher may claim the credit.

With respect to substantial rights under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2), if a taxpayer performing research for another person retains no substantial rights in research under the agreement providing for the research, the research is treated as fully funded for purposes of Section 41(d)(4)(H), and no expenses paid or incurred by the taxpayer in performing the research are qualified research expenses. Crucially, incidental benefits to the taxpayer from performance of the research, such as increased experience in a field of research or general know-how, do not constitute substantial rights, nor does a taxpayer retain substantial rights if the taxpayer must pay a royalty or fee for the right to use the results of the research. In Kilroy-style licensing or engineering arrangements, contracts that transfer full, exclusive ownership of patents or designs upon creation without reserving a royalty-free right to use the underlying technology create an immediate statutory whipsaw where either the researcher loses the credit for lack of substantial rights, or neither party obtains the credit when payment is also contingent on technical success.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and regulatory requirement implicated in Kilroy v. Commissioner and its related federal R&D tax credit jurisprudence against the specific taxpayer failures and the governing judicial standards of proof.

cells: Trade or Business Nexus & Profit Motive
I.R.C. § 174(a)(1); I.R.C. § 162(a); I.R.C. § 41(b)(1); Snow v. Commissioner, 416 U.S. 500 (1974); Kilroy v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1980-489

Conducting isolated, sporadic inventing activities without patent applications or marketing efforts (as in the taxpayer's unsuccessful earlier case, T.C. Memo. 1973-7); or acting as a passive investor/partnership that pre-assigns commercialization rights to an external operating entity.

Under § 174, the taxpayer must prove through objective facts an intent to engage in the business for profit—in Kilroy, shown by procuring numerous patents and making substantial marketing efforts over a period of years despite negligible receipts—and, under later case law, a "realistic prospect" (both objective intent and capability) of commercially exploiting the research results. Under § 41(b)(1), the taxpayer must already be actively "carrying on" the business when QREs are incurred.
Experimental Character vs. Routine Engineering / Exploration

Deducting routine mining exploration expenses (to locate or ascertain mineral deposit quality) or routine developmental engineering and equipment modifications where operational feasibility is not in doubt.

The taxpayer must prove that activities were conducted in the "experimental or laboratory sense" to resolve objective technological uncertainty regarding capability, method, or appropriate design of a product or patentable invention, strictly segregated from mineral exploration under § 617 and routine engineering.
Structured Process of Experimentation
I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)
Relying on ad-hoc trial and error, unrecorded engineering intuition, or routine adaptation/fit-testing without evaluating technical alternatives to eliminate scientific uncertainty.

The taxpayer must substantiate that "substantially all" () of research activities for each separate business component constituted elements of a systematic process of experimentation—identifying uncertainty, formulating hypotheses, modeling/simulating alternatives, and conducting scientific testing.
Indirect Cost Nexus (§ 174) vs. Direct QRE Scope (§ 41)

Claiming unallocated telephone utilities, travel, or overhead expenses under § 174 without proving proximate nexus to R&E; or erroneously including Kilroy-eligible indirect utilities and travel in the § 41 credit base.

Under § 174, indirect costs (heat, light, power, telephone utilities, travel, administrative overhead) are eligible (and, for 2022–2024 domestic expenditures and all foreign expenditures, subject to mandatory capitalization) to the extent they relate to R&E activities; Kilroy allowed the research-related percentage of office expenses based on a reasonable allocation under Cohan, although contemporaneous records remain the best defense against disallowance. Under § 41(b), all indirect, travel, and utility costs must be strictly excluded from QREs.
Contemporaneous Books and Records Substantiation
Presenting disorganized receipts, retrospective oral estimates, or lump-sum expense ledgers that fail to tie employee/inventor time and supply/utility outlays to specific qualified research projects.

The taxpayer bears the burden of maintaining organized, contemporaneous books, project time-tracking logs, lab notebooks, and itemized expense vouchers that establish a verifiable nexus between every dollar claimed and a qualified business component.
Economic Risk & Substantial Rights (Funded Research)

Entering into joint ventures, licensing deals, or engineering contracts where the researcher retains no substantial rights (e.g., work-for-hire or royalty-bearing license back) or where payment is guaranteed regardless of technical success.

To claim in-house QREs (or defeat funded exclusion), the researcher must prove via the four corners of the contract that payment is contingent on technical success and that the researcher retains substantial rights to use the research results without paying for that right. For contract research QREs, the payor must bear the financial risk of failure and hold a right to the research results.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To demonstrate the practical application of Kilroy v. Commissioner alongside current I.R.C. § 174 capitalization rules and I.R.C. § 41 research credit standards, the following two industry case studies examine realistic taxpayers confronting the exact legal pitfalls identified in the ruling, followed by comprehensive, step-by-step remedial restructuring protocols.
Case Study 1: Subsurface Extractive Robotics & Autonomous Mining Systems Venture
Factual Scenario and Audit Exposure

TerraVein Autonomous Systems LLC ("TerraVein") is a pre-revenue Delaware limited liability company taxed as a partnership, formed by two mechanical engineers to develop an autonomous hydraulic push-pull continuous rock-excavation system for hard-rock lithium mining. TerraVein has no salaried W-2 employees and leases no formal commercial office space; the two founder-managers conduct computer-aided design (CAD) modeling from home offices and perform field testing at a third-party mine site in Nevada owned by LithiumCorp, an unrelated mining operator.

TerraVein's operating and contractual structure exhibits four severe Kilroy and Section 41 vulnerabilities. First, regarding trade or business status and passive investment risk, TerraVein executed a Joint Venture and Option Agreement with LithiumCorp under which LithiumCorp provided a $500,000 advance and granted site access in exchange for an immediate, exclusive, royalty-bearing option to acquire all resulting patents upon completion of prototype testing. TerraVein possesses no independent business plan or operational capability to manufacture mining equipment or license the technology to other mines. Second, regarding technical commingling, while deployed at the Nevada site, TerraVein engineers spent 40 percent of their field time conducting core-drilling assays to map LithiumCorp's lithium vein concentrations—which constitutes routine mineral exploration excluded under I.R.C. § 174(c)(2)—and 60 percent testing experimental hydraulic thruster pressure tolerances, yet booked all outlays into a single general ledger account titled "Nevada Field Engineering". Third, regarding indirect cost substantiation, TerraVein claimed $180,000 in travel expenses, satellite telephone utilities, diesel fuel, and home-office power bills as both Section 174 R&E deductions and Section 41 QREs, supported only by unallocated credit card statements without project logs. Fourth, because TerraVein has no gross receipts and no W-2 wages, and because LithiumCorp's $500,000 advance is non-refundable while stripping TerraVein of substantial intellectual property rights, TerraVein faces total disallowance under both Section 174 passive investor doctrines and the Section 41(d)(4)(H) funded research exclusion.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Protocol
Step 1: Corporate Governance and Trade or Business Restructuring

To establish an active trade or business of inventing and technology licensing under Kilroy and IRS Field Attorney Advice 20055203F, TerraVein must terminate the single-buyer pre-assignment structure with LithiumCorp. TerraVein must adopt a formal Corporate Charter and Multi-Client Commercialization Plan documenting its objective intent and operational capability to exploit its excavation patents across the global mining industry through non-exclusive licensing and royalty agreements. Even without formal office space or manufacturing plants—which Kilroy did not treat as prerequisites, instead finding a trade or business from patent procurement and substantial marketing efforts sustained over a period of years—TerraVein must establish continuous commercial operations by maintaining dedicated corporate books, actively marketing its licensing portfolio to multiple mining conglomerates, and filing provisional and utility patent applications in its own name. Simultaneously, TerraVein must align its founder compensation structure—either by electing corporate tax status with W-2 salaries or by properly structuring self-employed earned income under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(D)—so that in-house technical labor constitutes statutory wages eligible for the Section 41(b)(4) start-up trade or business exception.
Step 2: Contractual Redrafting to Preserve Substantial Rights and Allocate Economic Risk

TerraVein and LithiumCorp must replace the Joint Venture and Option Agreement with a Site Access and Contingent Prototype Purchase Agreement governed by Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d). To preserve substantial rights, Section 4.1 of the revised contract must explicitly stipulate that TerraVein retains sole and exclusive legal title, ownership, and substantial rights in all background and foreground intellectual property, patents, trade secrets, and engineering designs developed under the agreement. LithiumCorp is granted only a non-exclusive license to operate the delivered prototype unit at its Nevada facility, while TerraVein retains the unfettered, royalty-free right to manufacture, sell, lease, or license the underlying push-pull mining technology to any third party without paying LithiumCorp for that right.

To shift financial risk onto TerraVein, Section 3.2 of the revised contract must mandate that LithiumCorp's $500,000 milestone payments are strictly contingent upon the prototype achieving objective technical barometers during formal inspection, evaluation, and acceptance testing—specifically, sustaining continuous hydraulic thrust in granite with less than seal degradation over a 72-hour continuous run. If the prototype fails acceptance testing, TerraVein is contractually obligated to refund the advance. This contractual structure converts the transaction into a contingent sale of a research result rather than funded research, preserving 100 percent of TerraVein's QRE eligibility under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H).
Step 3: Technical Segregation of Mining Exploration from Experimental Engineering

To overcome the I.R.C. § 174(c)(2) mining exploration exclusion, TerraVein's Chief Engineer must institute a strict chart-of-accounts bifurcation prior to field deployment. All core-drilling, ore assaying, and geological mapping activities aimed at locating or quantifying lithium deposits must be isolated into a dedicated general ledger account designated "Account 6100: Non-R&E Geological Exploration". These extractive costs are billed directly to LithiumCorp or accounted for under I.R.C. § 617, completely walled off from Section 174 and Section 41 tax claims. Conversely, a separate general ledger account designated "Account 7200: Experimental Mechanical & Hydraulic R&D" must capture exclusively those engineering activities dedicated to resolving technological uncertainty regarding the optimal hydraulic valve geometry and carbide cutter-head metallurgy required to prevent thermal seizure under high-load rock excavation.
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking and Dual-Ledger Cost Accounting

TerraVein must implement a digital project management and time-tracking system organized by specific Business Components, such as BC-01: High-Pressure Hydraulic Actuator Seal Assembly and BC-02: Autonomous Laser-Guided Steering Controller. For each component, engineers must contemporaneously record the specific technical uncertainty (such as standard elastomeric seals extruding at pressures exceeding under abrasive silica dust ingress), the scientific hypotheses formulated (such as testing multi-stage PTFE-bronze stepped backup rings against hydrostatic pressure-balanced labyrinth seals), and the Finite Element Analysis (FEA) simulation data and Nevada field test telemetry logs demonstrating systematic trial-and-error evaluation.

Simultaneously, TerraVein's tax advisor must maintain a Dual-Ledger Tax Accounting Matrix to properly apply Kilroy without violating Section 41. The first ledger, representing the I.R.C. § 174 Specified R&E Capitalization Pool, captures direct engineer compensation and prototype fabrication materials alongside indirect expenses validated under Kilroy—specifically satellite telephone logs documenting technical calls with hydraulic suppliers, travel expenses to the Nevada test site for prototype experimentation, and allocated utility power used to run hydraulic test rigs. Every indirect travel and telephone voucher must be stamped contemporaneously with a Business Component code and a brief technical purpose note to satisfy Kilroy's requirement that only the portion of indirect expenses relating to the research be included, and this total pool is deducted currently under I.R.C. § 174A for domestic expenditures in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024 (or, at TerraVein's election, capitalized and amortized over not less than 60 months under § 174A(c)), while any 2022–2024 domestic expenditures remain subject to five-year amortization under former § 174(a)(2)(B). The second ledger, representing the I.R.C. § 41 Qualified Research Expense Pool, strips out 100 percent of the Kilroy telephone utilities, travel expenses, and overhead costs, retaining strictly qualified direct wages, direct physical supplies consumed in fabricating the experimental seal prototypes, and cloud computing costs used directly for FEA simulations under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2).
Case Study 2: Custom Enterprise Software & Cloud Architecture Development Partnership
Factual Scenario and Audit Exposure

Apex Quant Analytics LP ("Apex") is a software development limited partnership formed by a group of financial investors and a lead software architect to develop a novel low-latency, quantum-resistant cryptographic routing protocol for high-frequency institutional clearinghouses. Apex employs no internal programming staff; instead, it subcontracts 100 percent of the software coding to CipherDev Inc., an unrelated domestic software engineering firm, while the lead software architect works from a personal residence incurring substantial fiber-optic telecommunications utilities, travel costs to industry conferences, and administrative expenses.

Apex and CipherDev face immediate disallowance across both Section 174 and Section 41 due to four structural defects rooted in Kilroy and related software R&D jurisprudence. First, at the partnership level, under the limited partnership agreement, once CipherDev completes the software, an affiliated operating corporation (Apex Clearing Corp.) holds a pre-wired, nominal-cost option to acquire the exclusive rights to commercialize the software. Under Kilroy, Green, and Snow, because Apex LP—unlike the taxpayer and his partnership in Kilroy, who themselves patented and marketed the inventions—never intended to market or license the software in its own trade or business, Apex LP is a passive investment conduit barred from both Section 174 deductions and Section 41 contract research credits. Second, regarding technical eligibility, the Statement of Work (SOW) between Apex and CipherDev describes the engagement as converting and migrating legacy C++ routing libraries to Rust and configuring standard TLS 1.3 encryption modules. Under Rev. Proc. 69-21, Rev. Proc. 2000-50, and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6), converting or adapting existing software where operational feasibility is not seriously in doubt fails both Section 174 and the Section 41 Four-Part Test.

Third, the Master Services Agreement (MSA) between Apex and CipherDev creates a fatal Section 41 Mirror Rule conflict. The MSA is a fixed-price $1.2 million contract payable only if the software passes final benchmark acceptance testing demonstrating cryptographic handshake latency below , yet Section 8 of the MSA assigns 100 percent of all intellectual property and source code exclusively to Apex upon creation, prohibiting CipherDev from reusing any architectural algorithms without paying a licensing fee. This triggers the exact statutory whipsaw analyzed in Section 41 legal literature: Apex cannot claim contract research QREs because payment is contingent on technical success (meaning Apex is purchasing a finished product rather than funding uncertain research), while CipherDev cannot claim in-house QREs because it retains no substantial rights in the research. Fourth, the lead architect deducted 100 percent of personal residential utility bills, cellular telephone plans, and travel to general trade shows as Section 174 expenses without any allocation methodology or documented technical nexus.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Protocol
Step 1: Restructuring Entity Governance to Establish an Active Licensing Trade or Business

To align with the favorable holding of Kilroy v. Commissioner and the joint-venture software guidelines established in federal tax practice, Apex LP must eliminate the pre-wired nominal option held by Apex Clearing Corp. and adopt one of two structural remedies. Under the first structural pathway, modeled directly on Kilroy, Apex LP restructures as an active intellectual property development and licensing enterprise in which the lead software architect serves as Managing General Partner with an active technical governance mandate. Apex LP retains legal ownership of all cryptographic patents and software know-how and executes an active commercialization strategy to license the software on a non-exclusive, recurring royalty basis to multiple institutional clearinghouses. Under the alternative structural pathway, Apex LP and Apex Clearing Corp. form an operating general partnership or joint venture LLC into which Apex Clearing Corp. contributes an ongoing, active software marketing and enterprise support business. Because the joint venture is actively "carrying on" an existing trade or business under I.R.C. § 162 and § 41(b)(1) during the research period, and contracts for the software development on its own behalf and at its own risk, both the Section 174 and Section 41 trade or business requirements are satisfied.
Step 2: Resolving the Section 41 Mirror Rule Whipsaw in the Master Services Agreement

Apex and CipherDev must consciously allocate the Section 41 tax credit to one party by amending the MSA to harmonize payment contingency with substantial rights under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e) and § 1.41-4A(d). If the parties intend to allocate the tax credit to Apex (or the operating joint venture) as the payor claiming contract research QREs, they must amend the MSA to a time-and-materials engineering services contract where Apex is unconditionally obligated to pay CipherDev for engineering hours worked regardless of whether the latency target is achieved. The amended contract must explicitly state that CipherDev performs the research on behalf of Apex, that Apex bears the sole financial risk of technical failure, and that Apex holds exclusive rights to the research results, thereby allowing Apex to claim 65 percent of the payments to CipherDev as qualified contract research expenses under I.R.C. § 41(b)(3).

Conversely, if the parties intend to allocate the credit to CipherDev as the researcher claiming in-house QREs, they must retain the fixed-price, success-contingent acceptance provisions—where CipherDev is paid only if the software satisfies strict inspection, evaluation, and latency barometers—and simultaneously amend Section 8 of the MSA so that CipherDev retains substantial rights in the underlying cryptographic routing architecture. Specifically, the amended IP clause must grant CipherDev a perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free right to commercialize, license, and deploy the core cryptographic libraries for any client outside the institutional clearinghouse sub-sector without paying a fee or royalty to Apex. Under this structure, CipherDev's research is un-funded under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H), enabling CipherDev to claim 100 percent of its eligible in-house W-2 developer wages and cloud testing supplies.
Step 3: Technical Re-Scoping from Routine Code Migration to Algorithmic Experimentation

To satisfy Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1) and I.R.C. § 41(d), the SOW and technical specifications must be redrafted to separate routine code conversion from genuine computer science experimentation. All routine migration of legacy C++ syntax to Rust and off-the-shelf TLS 1.3 configuration must be segregated into a non-qualifying "Maintenance & Porting" workstream. The qualified R&D workstream must be defined around a specific, documented Technological Uncertainty: because post-quantum lattice-based cryptographic keys (such as CRYSTALS-Kyber) increase payload sizes fifteen-fold over classical elliptic-curve keys, standard TCP/IP kernel packet processing causes buffer bloat and tail-latency spikes exceeding , rendering the optimal memory-allocation architecture and zero-copy kernel-bypass algorithm required to achieve deterministic latency unknown and unavailable in existing computer science literature.
Step 4: Contemporaneous Experimentation Tracking and Indirect Cost Allocation

To meet the Tax Court's strict substantiation standards under I.R.C. § 6001, software engineers must link every Git version-control commit, pull request, and Continuous Integration (CI/CD) benchmark run to a specific experimental hypothesis ticket, such as evaluating eBPF XDP kernel-bypass ring buffers against DPDK user-space polling under simulated 10Gbps burst traffic. Automated telemetry outputs capturing 99th-percentile latency distributions across failed and successful builds must be archived contemporaneously as objective proof of a systematic process of experimentation under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C).

For the lead software architect's indirect expenses under Section 174, Apex must establish a documented allocation methodology consistent with the research-related allocation of office expenses accepted in Kilroy. General residential electricity and personal cellular telephone bills must be excluded entirely. A dedicated commercial high-bandwidth fiber line installed exclusively to connect to the cloud testbed cluster must be documented with network usage logs demonstrating 100 percent R&E utilization. Travel expenses must be restricted strictly to trips where contemporaneous meeting minutes and engineering agendas prove the travel was undertaken to conduct joint architectural design reviews and hardware-in-the-loop testing at CipherDev's laboratory, excluding general marketing or trade-show attendance. These substantiated indirect utilities and travel costs are properly included in Apex's domestic research expenditures under I.R.C. § 174A (deductible currently for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, or capitalized and amortized over not less than 60 months if Apex so elects under § 174A(c)) while being rigorously excluded from the I.R.C. § 41 QRE credit computation.
5. Comprehensive Synthesis and Strategic Conclusions

The Tax Court's decision in Kilroy v. Commissioner provides enduring doctrinal clarity on two foundational questions in United States R&D tax law: first, that an independent inventor (and his family partnership) can be engaged in a valid "trade or business" of inventing under I.R.C. § 174 before receiving any income from it and while having substantial outside income, where, as there, the taxpayer procured numerous patents and made substantial marketing efforts over a period of years that evidenced a profit motive; and second, that the portion of office expenses relating to research activities falls within Section 174 (the Court noting its prior allowance of telephone, travel, and labor costs incurred in invention activities) and may be allocated on a reasonable basis under the Cohan rule where the record supports an allocation.

For modern tax counsel and technical advisors, however, applying Kilroy requires navigating a bifurcated statutory landscape where Section 174 and Section 41 diverge sharply in both operational scope and tax consequences. While Kilroy's inclusion of research-related office expenses historically benefited taxpayers seeking immediate current deductions, the post-2021 Section 174 capitalization regime transformed that broad scope into a mandatory capitalization obligation for indirect utilities, travel, and overhead that bear a direct relationship to research—an obligation that, since the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, continues for foreign research, while domestic research expenditures in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024 may again be deducted currently under I.R.C. § 174A. Conversely, when transitioning from Section 174 eligibility to computing the Section 41 tax credit, taxpayers must apply a strict statutory filter: stripping out all Kilroy indirect costs, verifying active trade or business operations (or strict statutory start-up compliance), segregating routine engineering and mineral exploration from scientific experimentation, and drafting R&D contracts that align payment contingency with substantial intellectual property rights. By integrating contemporaneous technical hypothesis tracking with disciplined contractual and cost-accounting segregation, taxpayers can simultaneously withstand IRS scrutiny under Kilroy and maximize defensible research credits under I.R.C. § 41.
